analysis.one_liner: Funded health insurance for uninsured low-income children with higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 1997 with 16 cosponsors, the bill was sent to three House committees and never received a vote in either chamber before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created federal grants to states to subsidize private health coverage for uninsured children in low- and moderate-income families, with benefits at least as rich as Medicaid or the largest federal employee health plan, plus an option to get care directly through community health centers. It would have paid for this by roughly tripling the federal cigarette tax and raising other tobacco taxes, with any money left over going to deficit reduction. It was referred to three House committees at once, sent to subcommittees, and never marked up, voted on, or brought to the floor; it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured children in low- and moderate-income working families — the bill targeted children who make too much to qualify for Medicaid but lack employer coverage. States would have received federal grants (from $3 billion in 1998 rising to $5 billion by 2001) to pay insurers at least 95 percent of premiums for families under 185 percent of the poverty line, with no cost-sharing for preventive care, and could contract directly with community health centers to serve enrolled children. Up to 5 percent of each state's funds could go to services for pregnant women, new mothers, and infants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured children in low-income working families

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $3 billion to $5 billion per year (fiscal years 1998-2002) in federal grants to states to subsidize health coverage for uninsured children, allocated by each state's share of uninsured eligible children.

Requires participating states to make coverage available to every eligible child that is either equivalent to Medicaid benefits or comparable to the largest-enrollment Federal Employees Health Benefits plan, with federal subsidies covering at least 95 percent of premiums for children in families below 185 percent of the poverty line and no cost-sharing on preventive services.

Lets states contract directly with community health centers to provide services to enrolled children as a direct-service alternative to private insurance, and allows up to 5 percent of a state's grant for programs serving pregnant women, new mothers, and infants.

Bars employers from conditioning or varying health coverage contributions because an employee's child qualifies for the subsidy, and bars states from cutting their own Medicaid child eligibility to shift costs onto the new program.

Pays for the program by increasing the federal cigarette tax from $12 to $33.50 per thousand (about 24 cents to 67 cents per pack), with similar increases on cigars, smokeless tobacco, and pipe tobacco, and dedicates revenue beyond the program's cost to reducing the federal deficit.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco companies and the people who buy tobacco products. The bill raises excise taxes on cigarettes (roughly tripling the per-pack federal tax), cigars, smokeless tobacco, pipe tobacco, cigarette papers and tubes, and imposes a one-time tax on tobacco inventory held when the increase takes effect. Excise taxes like this are typically passed through to consumers in higher prices, and smokers are disproportionately lower-income adults.

drawbacks.text: The funding mechanism is a tobacco tax, and tobacco taxes are regressive: smokers skew toward lower incomes, so many of the same working families the bill aims to help would pay more for cigarettes, including through a one-time floor-stocks tax on inventory held when the higher rates take effect.

The program is not an entitlement — the bill says so explicitly and lets a state narrow its income criteria or scale back the program if its grant money runs short, so coverage could be rationed rather than guaranteed.

A child is ineligible for assistance if anyone in the family had group health coverage in the previous six months, a waiting period designed to stop employers from dropping family coverage and shifting costs to the program, but one that leaves a six-month gap for families that just lost job-based coverage.
The subsidies are paid directly to health insurance issuers, routing a new public program through private insurers as the delivery channel rather than expanding a public program directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a large, targeted benefit — near-free comprehensive coverage for uninsured children just above the Medicaid line — paid for by a tax on a product that harms health, which also discourages smoking among children. That is a favorable trade on its face. The honest caveats are real but second-order: the tax falls partly on low-income smokers, the program is not an entitlement and can be scaled back if money runs short, and the six-month uninsured waiting period creates a gap for families who recently lost job-based coverage. It was a reasonably designed bill whose main design choice, using private insurers as the delivery channel, also gave insurers a new stream of subsidized customers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in House subcommittees from May 1997 until the Congress ended, and no committee, subcommittee, or floor vote was ever taken.

narrative.text: Nancy Johnson introduced the bill on April 17, 1997, with six original cosponsors from both parties, and the House referred it the same day to three committees at once — Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce — with the timing of consideration left to be determined by the Speaker.

Within three weeks it was sent down to subcommittees: the Health Subcommittee of Commerce, the Health and Environment Subcommittee, and the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee of Education and the Workforce.
No markup, hearing record in the bill's history, committee vote, or floor action ever followed. The 105th Congress ended January 3, 1999, with the bill still parked in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco companies are the clearest winner: the bill's roughly tripling of the federal cigarette tax never happened. The three House committees with jurisdiction also kept control over health and tobacco tax legislation without this bill moving, and uninsured children got nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies, which avoided the tax increase

for.name: Rep. Nancy L. Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor; the bill carried her name as author.

for.name: Original cosponsors: Reps. Robert Matsui (D-CA), Fortney 'Pete' Stark (D-CA), James McGovern (D-MA), Walter Riggs (R-NC), Constance Morella (R-MD), and Marge Roukema (R-NJ)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced, pairing Democrats on Ways and Means with Republicans to give the bill bipartisan weight.

for.name: 16 cosponsors (12 Democrats, 4 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Added their names to the bill during its first month, giving it more Democratic than Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Speaker of the House (Newt Gingrich)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to three committees simultaneously — Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce — with the period for consideration 'to be subsequently determined,' splitting its jurisdiction among committees.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership (Chair Thomas Bliley)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the full committee or its Health and Environment Subcommittee for a markup or vote after its April 1997 referral.

against.name: House Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce Committee leadership (Chairs Bill Archer and William Goodling)
against.role: Chairs of the other two referring committees
against.what_they_did: Also took no action on the bill after referral; neither committee marked it up or voted on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Manufacturers and sellers of tobacco products
against.what_they_did: Fought federal tobacco tax increases during the 1997-1998 tobacco debates.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 12 of the 16 cosponsors were Democrats — but the bill never reached a vote, so support and opposition never showed up on any roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have roughly tripled the federal cigarette excise tax (from $12 to $33.50 per thousand) and raised taxes on cigars, smokeless and pipe tobacco, plus a one-time tax on existing inventory. The industry's gain from the bill's failure was the public's loss in revenue for children's coverage.

States were required to contract with private insurance issuers, and premium subsidies were paid directly to the insurer, so the program would have delivered billions in new subsidized customers to insurers. Insurers would have had to guarantee availability and meet Medicaid-equivalent or federal-employee-plan benefit standards.

In every area served by a health center, states would have had to contract directly with the center to serve enrolled children who chose direct services, sending federal money to safety-net providers. This option ran alongside the private-insurance option, giving families a choice.

Employers could not condition or vary health contributions because an employee's child qualified for the subsidy, but they could not be forced to offer the qualifying policy, and the six-month uninsured waiting period was designed to prevent employers from dropping family coverage.
